differences.title: 1. ISOLATION MODEL
differences.leftDesc: Firecracker boots a minimalist Linux microVM with its own kernel and hardware device model. Containers run inside that VM, so isolation is enforced by VM boundaries, not merely process namespaces and seccomp filters.
differences.rightDesc: gVisor runs container workloads on top of a sandboxed “runsc” kernel implemented in user space. Instead of a VM boundary, it intercepts and mediates syscalls to prevent escapes and restrict resource access while sharing the host kernel.

differences.title: 2. BOOT & STARTUP
differences.leftDesc: Firecracker uses KVM to start a microVM quickly with a trimmed device set and snapshot-style flows. Startup latency is dominated by VM creation and kernel initialization, optimized for cloud scaling.
differences.rightDesc: gVisor avoids booting a guest kernel; it starts the sandbox runtime and then traps syscalls from the containerized process. Latency is typically lower than VM start because there’s no kernel boot path.

differences.title: 3. SYSCALL HANDLING
differences.leftDesc: Inside Firecracker, the workload talks to a real Linux kernel running in the microVM. The kernel executes syscalls normally, subject to VM constraints, cgroups, and device model permissions.
differences.rightDesc: gVisor translates syscalls in user space: runsc captures a syscall request, performs validation and policy checks, then emulates or proxies the behavior as permitted. Unsupported syscalls may fall back or be blocked depending on configuration.

differences.title: 4. HARDWARE & DEVICES
differences.leftDesc: Firecracker exposes a controlled set of emulated devices (e.g., virtio-net, block devices) via its microVM device model. This reduces the host attack surface because only defined virtual hardware is visible to the guest.
differences.rightDesc: gVisor maps filesystem and networking through the sandbox: it emulates or proxies aspects of device interactions to the host while keeping enforcement in user space. The guest doesn’t see a separate hardware device model.

differences.title: 5. ATTACK SURFACE & ESCAPE RISK
differences.leftDesc: Because Firecracker runs a separate kernel inside the microVM, exploits must cross the VM boundary in addition to conventional container isolation. This segmentation can significantly reduce host-level impact of a compromised workload.
differences.rightDesc: gVisor narrows escape pathways by handling syscalls in a controlled environment, but the host kernel still exists and is the foundation beneath runsc. Security depends on syscall coverage, correctness of emulation, and policy completeness.

differences.title: 6. PERFORMANCE TRADEOFFS
differences.leftDesc: Firecracker introduces virtualization costs: memory footprint, vCPU scheduling, and VM device emulation. However, syscall execution is native within the guest kernel, which can outperform heavy syscall-trapping approaches for many workloads.
differences.rightDesc: gVisor can add overhead from syscall interception and emulation/proxy paths. CPU cost often rises for syscall-heavy applications, and certain kernel features may not be fully supported, affecting performance and compatibility.

differences.title: 7. OPERATIONS & ECOSYSTEM
differences.leftDesc: Firecracker is commonly integrated via orchestration layers that treat the microVM as the execution unit, requiring image/boot artifacts and VM lifecycle management. Tuning focuses on kernel config, device model, and VM sizing.
differences.rightDesc: gVisor is typically deployed as a container runtime sandbox (e.g., via Kubernetes runtimeClass). Operators tune syscall policy, filesystem/network handling, and compatibility settings, while keeping the familiar container image workflow.
